subtopic: PRISONERS OF WAR IN JAPAN
speechtext:

subtopic: ENLISTMENT CAMPAIGN
ENLISTMENT CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
What has the government done towards launching a nation-wide enlistment campaign in
the weeks preceding the plebiscite and obtaining the fullest participation of all members of parliament in such a recruiting drive?

subtopic: ENLISTMENT CAMPAIGN
speechtext: May I answer this question orally? It is not the intention, as I am at present advised, to launch what might be called a special campaign in the weeks preceding the plebiscite. I can say, however, that we have been and shall be carrying on a nation-wide enlistment campaign, to use the words of the question, continuously, day in and day out. The house will probably be interested to know, if I may put it on the record now, the response we have had to date this year. In January the recruiting figures for the army were, as I believe I told the house, about 11,700; in February, a short month, 8,152; and in March up to and including the 14th, 4,019 for a little less than half a month. Regarding the participation of members of parliament, I may say first that citizens' committees all over the country have been exceedingly helpful and are increasing their activities. As I have said to the house before, the work of getting men for the armed forces justifies the very best efforts of all of us and I wish to emphasize again what I consider to be the need for the fullest and most active participation of all members of parliament in that effort. I venture to think that it is one of the many duties that rest upon members of this house in connection with their responsibilities of leadership.

When the house adjourned at six o'clock on Friday last I was endeavouring to show that all the proposals which might be formulated by the government concerning this subject must be directed toward the solution of two important problems of agriculture: one, debt and taxation; the other, the exploitation or exhaustion of the soil.
This policy, having been formulated, I believe that the farmer's responsibility ends there, and the responsibility of his elected members, his government, begins. It is then the duty or responsibility of his government to formulate plans which might be designed to achieve the results sought. Because of this we must have a policy, and if this policy is to be effective it must be based entirely upon the financing of consumption.
Farmers do not need to be told how to raise products. There are far too many government departments telling him how he must or must not do certain things. Farmers as a body have learned agriculture in the school of bitter experience. What they really want to know is how to sell the output of their farms and obtain an adequate return for their labour, so that in the course of a normal year they can make a decent income from working and managing their farms. In other words the farmers want to know how to pay their debts and give their families a decent standard of living. That, to me, is the farm problem, stripped of all verbiage and trimmings. AVhen the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was speaking just a week ago to-day he said, as reported at page 1241 of Hansard:
As I said last year when we were asking them to do it, it took at least a hundred million dollars out of their pockets, and we did not by any means manage to put all of it back in.
Do hon. members realize what this implies? It means that the farmers of western Canada had $100 million less, which they could have used, which they could have applied upon their mortgages or bank loans and taxes. I did not
see in any newspaper, nor did I hear of any statement having been made by the Minister of Agriculture, that the minister would ask these financial institutions to ease their pressure on the farmer in the event of his not being able to meet his obligations. It would have been a humane gesture on the part of the Minister of Agriculture had he gone to the mortgage companies and other financial institutions and asked them to write off fifty per cent of this $100 million-or $50 million; split fifty-fifty, so to speak, on this amount of money. All the farmers received were left-handed compliments. No legislation was brought down to protect them against unfair or unscrupulous treatment on the part of the institutions or the municipalities.
A vital fact which is not recognized, so far as I am aware, in any policy of any government, is that the aptitude to produce requires a balancing facility for consuming. We can measure the wealth, the progress and the prosperity of agriculture only by what it sells. The whole aim of agriculture is to satisfy the needs of the people. These two ideas are constantly being lost sight You cannot have a state of over-production if potential output is governed by total effective consumption. Agriculture would face no serious difficulties if it were governed by this economic law rather than by government departments. Agriculture has been too long restricted because the purchasing power of the people has been restricted. Neither the restriction of production nor the restriction of consumers' purchasing power is pardonable as long as there is one home in the whole of the British empire, or in any of the allied countries, lacking agricultural commodities.
In 1939, when the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture were being discussed, I brought to his attention the plan devised by Milo Perkins of the United States department of agriculture. It is known as the "food stamp plan", and is intended solely for the purpose of dealing with surplus food commodities in that country. It is based upon the maxim that "charity begins at home". It is a scheme under which certain people may buy additional food at low prices, instead of that food being exported at cut rates. A subsidy is paid to the food merchant. The subsidy is paid out of taxes, and the scheme will increase taxation in direct proportion to its success. Apart from this feature, the plan employs the mechanism of Major Douglas's "just price". Not very long ago there appeared in the columns of the Western Producer a small news item, as follows:
Blue food stamps added $9,637,000 worth of farm products to the diets of nearly 3,600,000 persons in the United States during the month of September.
Wheat Board Act

In other words during the month of September, 1941, through the food stamp plan, the department of agriculture was able to distribute to the people of the United States $9,637,000 worth of farm products over and above normal consumption. In 1940 the consumption of meat increased by four pounds per capita over the year 1939. The consumption of pork in 1940 increased by 4-4 pounds per capita over the preceding year, which was the highest on record since 1929. The consumption of lard also increased, as was the case with many other agricultural products; and these increases were due to an increase in the purchasing power of the consuming public. On March 1, 1935, the editorial columns of the London Times contained this statement:
. The principal obstacle to trade revival lies in the inability of many potential customers to obtain the wherewithal to purchase commodities that they could use with advantage.
Again in 1940 the same newspaper carried this item:
Attempts in the past to get the economic machine back into gear have gone awry because we thought it enough to organize and stimulate production, bringing upon ourselves the anomalies of under-consumption" and "poverty in the midst of plenty." The consumer has too long been the stepchild both of economists and politicians. What will be needed most of all when peace is restored is planned consumption.
I recommend to the Minister of Agriculture close study of these two statements. I am sure no one, even in his weakest moments, would accuse the editor of the London Times of having a leaning toward such unorthodox views as those held by the Social Credit party; yet I want to repeat that the editor of this newspaper says that we must have planned consumption. We in this corner of the house have been advocating that for a considerable number of years. The financing of consumption must be studied, and we must come to it eventually. We must formulate a policy which, while acceptable to the agricultural community as a whole, also must be acceptable to the general public. Therefore I should like to suggest the following policy for agriculture: That Canadians as a whole should be provided with a flow of purchasing power adequate to ensure the distribution of as much as we can produce, and for which potential demand evists; that in the use of this purchasing power individuals shall be free to exercise their choice, and that farmers will be free from restriction and. control in order to fulfil the demand; and that the measures taken to put this policy into effect shall not be such as to cause an increase in taxation or debt, or an undue rise in price.

Here is where I should like to offer a suggestion to some of the farm organizations. I believe all these resolutions they have passed are very fine, but they should contain a clause which would safeguard their proposals. I maintain that the Minister of Agriculture could give $1 a bushel for wheat, or even SI.25, with one hand and a week from to-day turn around and increase the levy on every bushel of grain marketed from one per cent to five or even ten per cent. I have a feeling that he is even considering such a thing at the present time. Thus far I have not seen any safeguard such as I suggest should be in these resolutions.
No doubt many of my Liberal friends are extremely anxious to know what I would do about this matter. It is this. If I were made a dictator for the purpose of doing only one thing as a contribution to the "good life", I know what I would do. I would put the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the members of the agriculture committee into a room together and keep them there until they had settled the problems of food production and food distribution in this country. The only person for whom I would allow them to send to help in their deliberations would be the governor of the Bank of Canada. The penalty for not getting the job done would not be that they should be called honest men, but that they should be fired.
In case some hon. members may be inclined to attribute this very sensible idea to me, thereby consigning it to the grave as soon as it has been given birth, I hasten to advise those hon. members that it is not original by any means. In the Sunday Times of London England, two or three years ago there appeared an article written by .Lord Horder. I lifted bodily from that article the portion I have just read to the house, and paraphrased it to suit the present occasion. Lord Horder is one of the few individuals in Great Britain who received his title for sheer merit. He holds a most imposing number of public offices, and is in fact physician to the king. Because of his standing and international reputation this idea of his should be worthy of a trial.
In conclusion I desire to submit to the Minister of Agriculture the following recommendations:
1. As the policies recommended by the bureaucrats of the Department of Agriculture in the past years have not solved our agricultural problem, the services of these individuals should be dispensed with forthwith.
A thorough housecleaning in that department is in the public interest.

Wheat Board Act
2.	That all existing agricultural legislation, including t'he bill now under discussion, be wiped off the statute books, because they are mere palliatives, are costly to administer, and have lamentably failed in their purpose.
3.	That the committee on agriculture should sit continuously during the present session, and during all recesses, until a .permanent solution has been found.
4.	That this committee on agriculture should decide, first of all, what the actual problems of agriculture are, bearing in mind those I have mentioned, namely debt and its twin evil taxation, and the exhaustion or exploitation of t'he soil.
5.	That this committee formulate a policy which, if put into effect, will bring about quickly a permanent solution of these problems.
I would suggest that a study be made of two things: (a) financing consumption, and (b) the food stamp plan.
6.	That experts be appointed to administer the policy; that these experts be divorced entirely from political influence; and that in the event of the policies being successful these experts be appointed' to the positions in the department made vacant by the removal from office of those who have had charge of our agricultural policy over the years.
The outline of procedure I have given would make a real approach to 'this whole problem, and in my judgment would return agriculture to its rightful position in the economy of our country.

Mr. Speaker, at the last sitting of the house, I was prevented from voicing the honest and free views of the electors, both men and women, of my constituency of Laval-Two Mountains. Like our gallant soldiers at Hong Kong, I was a target, not for Japanese shells or other enemy missiles, but for the satirical shafts of the honourable the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) who is no longer, thank God, at the head of the Department of National Defence. However it may be, the affray has left me unscathed and in better fighting trim than ever.
Before proceeding with my remarks on the amendment and the measure now before the house, I wish to add my humble tribute to those paid by the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. members for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) and for Outremont (Mr. Yien) to the memory of the Right Hon. Senator Raoul Dandurand. That outstanding statesman has
passed away at a ripe old age, after a life marked by great achievements. May I recall one event in his long and brilliant career? Fifteen years have elapsed since the day when, at the Luxembourg Palace, speaking after Mr. Raymond Poincare, he thrilled the heart of a great nation. The experienced diplomat whom Canada mourns to-day had, like us, a passionate love of France. He ardently hoped for the liberation and resurrection of that great nation made immortal through centuries of sacrifice, genius and heroism.
His splendid, noble and great life will ever survive in our memory. May he rest in peace and may this Canadian soil which he loved so dearly shelter his eternal sleep.
Another outstanding citizen, Mr. Ernest Ayers, manufacturer and commander of the Order of Saint Gregory the Great, has recently died. A man noted for his boundless generosity, he had, together with his brother Harry, recently made to the town he loved so much, Lachute, the gift of a splendid temple dedicated to our Roman Catholic faith.
To the families of those two great Canadians I tender my heartfelt sympathy.
I also wish to offer my sincere condolence to the bereaved family of the Hon. Senator Edgar N. Rhodes, a former speaker of this house and minister of the crown.
Mr. Speaker, I would not have spoken in this debate had not some facts of national importance just been misrepresented in the Quebec assembly, in connection with the mobilization act and the repeated requests which, with a few of my fellow members, I have voiced in this parliament regarding exemption for farmers' sons.
For an obvious purpose of political propaganda, one of the ministers of the Quebec provincial government has dared to claim that Premier Godbout verbally requested the federal authorities, as early as 1939, to exempt farmers' sons from military service. What kind of people does this minister think the electors of our province are? He knows or ought to know that compulsory military service was only enacted in June, 1940. He cannot be unaware of the fact that the mobilization act was not passed by the dominion parliament until June 19, 1940. In this connection, I may refer Premier Godbout and his minister, Mr. Casgrain, to the official report of the House of Commons for June 19, 1940.
No, Mr. Speaker, Hon. Mr. Godbout did not ask that farmers' sons be exempted. On the contrary, he, along with his ministers and the members who support him, bitterly

opposed the motion which Mr. Rene Chalout moved in the Quebec assembly on June 18, 1940. That motion opposed the mobilization act. And while I and the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) were opposing with the utmost energy the mobilization act in the dominion parliament, Hon. Mr. Godbout lost no time in sending, on June 18, 1940, to our dominion ministers, a telegram wherein he rejoiced at the defeat of Mr. Chalout's motion. By such action he betrayed once more the farmers as well as the farmers' sons, who were later taken from the farms and sent to training camps under the mobilization act which had the hearty support of Mr. Godbout. No, a thousand times no! The premier of the province of Quebec has, with his supporters, championed the mobilization act by his vote. By his attitude and his actions, he supported in the Quebec assembly that act which now threatens to undermine agriculture, our first line of defence.
Let us now examine the correspondence that passed between the dominion government and Hon. Mr. Godbout. The letters written by Hon. Mr. Godbout, were belated and worthless, and they have had absolutely no effect upon the dominion government. Will that teach the Quebec premier that although retribution for servility and flattery may be late in coming it must inevitably sooner or later, bring shame upon dispensers of election bribes, upon people who break their promises one after the other and who have not the slightest regal'd for their pledged word. I say servility and flattery. Yet even these words are not biting enough to fully qualify the ambiguous and shameful attitude of the Quebec premier on the vital question of exemptions from military service for our farmers.
This man who sets himself up as the protector of agriculture waits a whole long year before broaching the matter to the federal authorities. You will easily note by the replies he received from Ottawa to what extent the premier of Quebec has become the ridiculous puppet of the dominion government. The Hon. Mr. Godbout wrote letters of the palest pink to both the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). All this is evident from the letter he addressed to the right hon. Prime Minister on February 3 last. He, the self-styled defender of the agricultural class, dared to congratulate the prime minister of this country for a speech in which the latter repudiated those very pledges that were the only safeguard of our farm youth, the only factor safeguarding agricultural production so vital to our defence.

The people will understand now why the government of Quebec, placed as is the federal administration under the thumb of high finance, has mobilized its millionaire friends, its election parasites, its vote "telegraphers" from Montreal and Quebec to steal the recent Quebec East and Montreal-St. Mary contests. All this rabble will henceforth work under the orders of J. A. A. Leclair, chief organizer for the Quebec provincial government.

Wheat Board Act

What has been the attitude of Mr. Godbout when wheat was brought east to the advantage of eastern farmers? Always influenced by the millers', the bakers' and the fertilizers' trusts, he has, for a number of years, refused to contribute to the transportation of western wheat into our province. The decision he took was only half-hearted. Being taken too late, it never attained its object. The hideous influence of the trust was exercised on the farmers of Quebec-those of Pontiac with the others-who have now to pay $38 a ton for fattening feed, while the consumer has to buy wheat flour at nearly $4 a hundred-weight. Such is the so-called protector of agriculture as our population should know him.
Will this man fell our people the name of the member of a trust, the financial grandee, who has just fled to the Bahama Islands with his assets in order to avoid the inconveniences of Canada's war effort and defence? Will he say how much in succession duties he caused the province of Quebec to lose?
Mr. Speaker, once again, and this is not the last time, I demand exemption from military service for farmers' sons. At this late hour, the premier of the province of Quebec claims that they should be exempted during the summer only. This is another deplorable mistake. Who would then attend, in the spring, to the daily stocks, to the growing of vegetable seedlings in hotbeds, to the tapping of maple trees?

Mr. Speaker, it was not my
intention to take part in this debate. The policy which the government finally submitted to the house, as embodied in the three measures which have been under consideration-two of which have had their second reading, and the third of which concerns the present debate- was so fully placed before the house by my colleagues the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon.) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that there was little required to be said in explanation of the measures; and I would not have risen from my seat to-day had it not been for some remarks made by a fellow-member from Manitoba, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), with which I shall deal presently.
Generally speaking, the policies which the government submitted in the measures which have been before the house were reached only after very long and careful consideration. Quite naturally they were conditioned by the state of war in which the country has been, is now and probably will be for some considerable time. War makes new demands and creates new situations from day to day, almost from hour to hour. There is no doubt that the success that Japan has achieved since she went to war on December 7 has greatly influenced the whole question of food supplies for Great Britain and her armies and for our other allies, or such of them as can be supplied. It is only necessary in that respect to reinforce what was said by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that a very large quantity of fats and oils, upon

Wheat Board Act
which our modern civilization so much depends, was derived from areas that are now under the control of Japan. But that was not the only disadvantage that came from Japan's success.
As is well known, Britain draws large supplies of foodstuffs, much of it concentrated like dairy products and canned goods, from Australia and New Zealand. We have to face the definite possibility that shipments from these two countries now will be very seriously interfered with, if not entirely shut off. The success that Japan has had in taking Singapore and overrunning Java has given her the bases from which she can range the south Pacific and the Indian ocean, and difficulties of convoying ships containing materials and foodstuffs from distant lands like Australia to the theatre of war in Europe have been tremendously increased. That means that Britain more and more must draw largely from north America for her supplies for her civilian population and her armies, and for some of the other allies as well, like the Free French. Consequently our policies have been shaped in the light of that inescapable fact.
In this country we must as far as possible increase the production of concentrated foods. What do I mean by concentrated foods? Bacon products, meat products, dairy products and, as far as possible, canned fish, fruits and vegetables. It is in the light of that fact that our policies were finally reached.
The question of wheat is not a new one in this house. Hon. members are well aware of that fact. I think I may modestly claim that for at least thirty-five years, indeed almost forty years, I have been directly or indirectly associated closely with the marketing of wheat from the plains of western Canada. I remember the time-it is so many years ago now that I do not like to recall it-when I managed a farmers' elevator in a little Manitoba country town and received there my first introduction to the problems of marketing wheat, and I recall also the agitation that took place in the early years of this century, which led to the creation of the first farmers' marketing company. All down through the years, from that time on, I have had a close association with the marketing problems in connection with wheat. I hesitate to make this statement, because one is reluctant to obtrude one's own personal views too much in a debate of this kind, but looking back over that period, while my judgment at times may have been wrong, I can quite conscientiously say that in all aspects relating to this problem I have endeavoured to do the thing which I thought was in the best interests of the farmers of western Canada.
If I may say so, I resent implications or insinuations that other motives have guided my conduct at any time during that long period of years.
The problem of marketing wheat is a difficult one because wheat is grown over an immense area by many scores of thousands of farmers, and naturally when a farmer is marketing his product under conditions where it passes for a time from his own hands before he gets settlement finally for it, there is room in his mind for doubt as to what may happen to it. I think it is unfortunate that this problem of marketing wheat in the past has not been free at times from political considerations or factors that operated in connection with it, and which often arose from people who were perfectly sincere. But I want to come back for a moment to the general line of policy that we have laid down.
As the bill indicates, we are limiting deliveries of wheat this year to 280 million bushels. It is quite unlikely, from the present outlook, that that quantity will be reached for marketing by the farmers of western Canada, and I say that for two or three reasons. In the first place, the subsoil moisture conditions in Saskatchewan and Alberta are worse than they have been for a good many years, and Saskatchewan and Alberta are provinces from which very largely, in fact almost entirely, wheat production comes. For a good many years now experience has shown that when, subsoil moisture conditions in the autumn are seriously deficient it is very unlikely that a bumper crop will be harvested. While therefore we will accept 280 million bushels, it appears to me doubtful to say the least whether that quantity will be reached.
But there was pressing need for the production of feeding grains. Last year there was a deficiency in feeding grains, that is in grains such as oats, barley and corn. The vast hog production campaign to meet the requirements of Britain, in which this country has been engaged for two years and which will require an increase of 140 million pounds of bacon products in 1942 over 1941, if we are to meet the requests that have been made to us by the British government, means that a very large increase must take place in the production of feeding grains. Not only that, but we shall probably be able to market in the United States, as has already been indicated by ministers who have preceded me, any surplus in these feeding grains that we can produce.
The United States, to make up a deficiency in vegetable oils and fats, is planning a quite considerable campaign for the planting of soya beans so that they may get from that
Wheat Board Act

source the vegetable oils necessary for their ordinary economy. For the same reason, as outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, we are giving encouragement to the increase of flax production in Canada. We hope to increase it at least fourfold in the present year. That is the explanation of the much higher price that is offered for flax than that at which it had been selling during the last few years.
Our policy then is to stimulate and increase the production of feeding grains. A year ago, when we were considering this problem, the prices for oats and barley, two of our main feeding grains, were at least 20 cents a bushel less than to-day. By the higher price now obtained for these grains, by establishing minimum prices for them, by the bonus which is paid per acre for their production on the basis of the 1940 wheat acreage, we hope that in the area capable of growing these feed grains we can very greatly increase their production. For this reason the bonus has been given. I think it is sound policy, notwithstanding some criticism of it in the house.
There is another aspect of our wheat production that requires consideration. There are many farmers in western Canada who would prefer to see any assistance they may receive from the government given on a bushel basis. Naturally those are the farmers living in what might be described as fairly sure crop areas. Their wishes have been met, though not to the extent that many of us would like to see, by the increase in the initial price from 70 to 90 cents a bushel. But on top of that we have retained the principle embodied in the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which in my judgment was one of the best pieces of legislation ever passed by this house in relation to this whole wheat problem. It is no secret that the credit for it goes very largely indeed to the present Minister of Agriculture. A farmer may suffer from total or partial crop failure through no fault of his own. It may be due to lack of rain- a crop lost through no fault of the farmer, indeed is usually or almost entirely due to lack of rain; it may be due to infestation with rust. In any case the farmer who thus finds his work lost and is left largely without any crop gets a measure of assistance under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. When we weigh all the factors involved I think the government, in the legislation submitted to the house, has in very large measure met the needs of the situation. I know that statement does not fit in with the views held by some hon. members opposite from western Canada. But as was said the other day in 
this debate, Canada is a large country and a difficult country to govern. No one section of Canada can always get everything it wants; otherwise government in the country would be impossible. I have long held the view, and I have been criticized for it and my position has been misrepresented in certain places, that any policies adopted for the protection of the wheat farmer in western Canada must carry the reasonable judgment not only of hon. members of this house but of the whole of Canada. I think that is a fair statement.
I should like now for a few moments to deal with some of the criticisms directed against me the other day by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). Let me say at once that the hon. member for Portage la Prairie is one of the sincerest members in this house. I have always said that, and I have always believed it; I do not -think there is any hon. member who tries more sincerely to do what he thinks is right. But at the same time, and I do not say it unkindly, there are very few hon. members in this house whose judgment is more influenced by their prejudices than my hon. friend. May I say to him and to the house that long experience in life has taught me this lesson, that prejudice is never other than a very poor substitute for reason.

Thirty years ago there was a very considerable agitation among the farmers of western Canada for a sample market in Winnipeg. If my hon. friends will go back and read the reports of the conventions of the grain growers associations in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba of thirty years ago-and I attended them all -they will see that this was often one of the principal topics of discussion. Why? Because on the Minneapolis market a few hundred miles south of Winnipeg they had what was called a sample market. They had a grading system, but they also had a sample market where any miller, buyer or dealer could go and examine samples of grain, and to my own knowledge premiums of as much as five or six cents a bushel were paid to certain farmers on certain grades. The point I wish to make is that prior to this limitation being placed in the grain act there had been mixing of grain all down through the years, and exception had not been taken to it. The difficulty arose in this way, and from a wholly different cause. The view developed in western Canada that on the average the grain shipped from the plains of the west was not equal in quality to the grain of twenty years before, and that was true. It was claimed that the mixing of grain had deteriorated the quality and lowered the general average of the grain reaching the markets abroad. That did not apply in the early years. Why did the difficulty arise at that time? I submit, Mr. Speaker, and I think I am well within the facts when I say, that it was due altogether to a great increase in the varieties of wheat produced in the west.
Let me give an illustration. About ten years ago I was motoring through Manitoba during harvest time, in the Neepawa district. There I saw a lovely field of wheat that looked to me to be good for thirty bushels to the acre. There had been some rust that year, and my instinct as an old grain man prompted me to stop the car and go into the field to see what damage had resulted from rust. The farmer was stooking a little distance away, and when my friend and I went into the field he came over. The gentleman with me was an experienced seedman. Before the farmer came over we picked up some heads and looked at them, and my friend said, "I have spotted seven different varieties of wheat in this one shock of grain." There was marquis, there was preston, there was red bobs, and I have forgotten the others. That practice was very widespread throughout the west. Many in this house will remember, and I am sure no one better than the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, the discussions that took place with regard to garnet wheat.

Wheat Board Act

of garnet wheat in western Canada was one of the greatest misfortunes ever to happen to the whole wheat business of the west. Consequently you had this mixture of varieties, and it is only within recent years that the seed branches, not only of the federal department but of the provincial departments of agriculture, have been emphasizing the need of pure seed. It was this mixing of varieties, many of which had altogether different milling qualities, that lowered the general standard of our wheat abroad, and it will not come back until we return to and maintain true varieties. This question came up largely because of that situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASED RATE PER BUSHEL ON WHEAT DELIVERED BY PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who spoke twice, to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar), and to a number of other hon. members on the government side, one cannot help but wonder whether we realize that agriculture is playing an important role in this war. The present government has met all other industries at least half way, but it has always chosen to turn a deaf ear to agriculture.
I should like to have the government tell us from whom it takes direction when it formulates its agricultural policies. I should like an answer to that question. In connection with other industries the government has acted upon representations made to it, but it has refused to do likewise in the case of the farmers. Just the other day the Minister of Agriculture suggested to the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) that he should go through his constituency and tell the people to accept the present wheat policy. Referring to the hon. member for Battle River, this is what the minister said, as reported on page 1211 of Hansard:
I would say to him that any member of this house who carries back into western Canada the government's policy in relation to wheat and its policy in relation to other farm products can stand before any audience and explain to the people there that this is the best that can be done under the conditions with which we are confronted in the Dominion of Canada to-day, and the best that has been done in an attempt to settle their problems at any time.
After reading that statement and after listening to the Minister of Agriculture, I begin to wonder whether the principle of

Wheat Board Act

democracy is being followed. He is asking bon. members to go out into their constituencies and tell the people what is good for them. I believe that any democratic government should take direction from the people; the people should tell the government what results they want, and then it is up to the government to get those results for the people. The government should not shove down their throats something they do not like, something against which they protest.
Agriculture is as important to our war effort as is the supply of man-power and the industries which are turning out the tools of war. As a matter of fact, agriculture is an inseparable part of our war effort. Our farmers are asked to feed those who are actually doing the fighting. They must also feed the men and women who turn the wheels of industry. According to a pamphlet issued by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, over two million Canadians are directly dependent upon agriculture for their livelihood. An additional three millions are indirectly dependent upon agriculture. That makes a total of over five million people, or approximately half our total population. The income of our farmers in the last few years has been around 10 per cent of the total national income; it should be 33 per cent, as it was between 1926 and 1929. This leaves the farmers an insufficient amount of purchasing power to carry on and be able to contribute their maximum to the war effort; they must also provide for the education of their children, and build security for themselves so that when they reach the failing years of their lives they will not be dependent upon charity.
The government's policy as announced by the two ministers is not good enough, despite the fact that three members of the cabinet have spoken in glowing terms about it. Farmers cannot pay debts with the answers which ministers have given this house; their creditors ask for cold cash.
My humble contribution in this debate will be to place before the government 'the views of the constituents whom I have the honour to represent. Some hon. member's may wonder why I speak of placing the views of my constituents before this house, and not merely personal views-which has been the practice of most hon. members. The explanation is this. Before leaving for Ottawa in January, and knowing that this session would be an important one, I decided to try out a bit of democracy, of which we hear so much though it is seldom practised. I called two one-day conventions at central points in my constituency for the purpose of discussing agricultural problems only. I asked both conventions to 
give me their instructions and promised to place their requests, or if you like, demands, before this house. That is precisely what I intend to do to-day. I wonder how many other hon. members, especially those on the government side, asked their constituents for instructions, and how many would dare put them before this house. Probably few, or maybe none, except the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). The reason is that hon. members on the government side who represent agricultural constituencies are putting their party before the interests of the farmers whom they represent. I am sure the farmers will pass their own judgment upon this attitude.
Coming back to the two conventions to which I referred, I would say that both were non-party affairs. All had equal privileges of voting, regardless of political affiliations. Over five hundred delegates attended the convention held in the town of Mundare and over four hundred and twenty were present in the town of Smoky Lake. They embodied their requests in the three resolutions which I shall read to the house. Let me read, first, the one regarding wheat. It states the points of importance probably as well as they have been put in this house:
Whereas wheat production is the foundation of Canadian agriculture and, in turn, agriculture is the basis of the national economy;
Whereas the havoc of war will create grave after-war problems, and the accumulation of adequate wheat reserves to meet the famine and pestilence which are likely to develop should be an essential feature of Canadian policy;
And whereas the stabilization of wheat production at an adequate level, and the efficiency of our entire national economy and the health of national morale are dependent upon farmers receiving a price which will cover production costs and provide a margin of profit for their services to the nation;
Therefore be it resolved by this non-party convention of farmers that the federal government forthwith provide for wheat prices to be stabilized at $1 per bushel at the nearest point of delivery on the basis of the average 1940 general price level and that it be varied to bear the same ratio to any rise in the general price level.
I do not think I need add anything to that resolution; it is self-explanatory.
I mentioned a moment ago something about democracy and parliament. I should like to say just an additional word or two. Parliament, in my opinion, is a body of men who are elected by the people and whose duty it is to place before the government the views of their constituents and press for results

Wheat Board Act
which the people demand. When hon. members place before parliament the demands of the people, it is up to the government to find ways and means of obtaining the required result. The people do not care how this result is achieved; but if the government cannot do it, they will be replaced by another government which will. When a government gives the people something against which they are protesting, surely it cannot claim to be a democratic government. While I am on this point of democracy, listen to what Aristotle had to say about it:
The best material of democracy is an agricultural population; there is no difficulty in forming a democracy where the mass of the people live by agriculture . . . not having the necessities of life they are always at work, and do not covet the property of others. . . . Next best to agricultural and in many respects similar are pastoral people. . . . The people of whom other democracies consist are far inferior to them.
It will be seen that Aristotle speaks highly of agriculturists. If we had more farmers in this house, perhaps the results would be different.
With regard to the primary producer, is it not phenomenal that the only people in the dominion whose markets are not protected are the primary producers? The farmer is always told how much he will get for the things he produces and he is also told how much he must pay for the things he buys. How can anyone explain this strange situation? The farmer or printary producer is again the only one who pays freight both ways; he pays freight on everything he sells and he pays freight on everything he buys. I could1 find in my desk a pre-election campaign leaflet to show that the government's candidate promised the people of the constituency that the present government would adjust freight rates and overhaul the whole freight rate structure. But here we are in the third session and' nothing has been done in that regard. Let me stress this point. It is not a matter of advancing arguments against the government or of the minister trying to tie up somebody on the opposition side. The problems that face us are serious. Surely we must realize that half of our total population is affected by agriculture and by the income derived therefrom. The farmers have no other income, and we .cannot expect them to take it on the chin year after year just because the government chooses to force down their throats some orthodox policy to which it wishes to cling.	[DOT]
I do not wish to blame the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I could not blame the Minister of Agriculture or even the Minister
of Finance, for they are only the Charlie McCarthys of the present financial system which dictates its policies to them and, of course, they have to carry them out to the letter. I will not say much about the income of the farmer because so many have already done so. The government seems to take a good deal of credit for the increased prices on bacon, butter, eggs and other commodities that have gone up. If the government could figure out some way which would give them an excuse to take that increase away from the farmers it certainly would. That has been the experience of the past.
In the Ottawa Citizen of January 31, 1942, in the column "Diary of our own Pepys", this is what the writer has to say:
All ir.orning busy at many matters, and all! afternoon, and so past six to the meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to see what I could hear about the farming situation and one of the things I heard was that in the last war the farmers got one-third of the national income and the rest of us two-thirds, whereas in this war they get only one-tenth and the rest of us nine-tenths.
And so on. That is only one little article which explains the situation. Again, in the Citizen of January 31, 1942, the following appears in an editorial:
In the last twenty years the farmers of Canada have laboured under heavy handicaps. Under deflation and negative politics agriculture has suffered more than any other single industry. For one thing farm income has dwindled to such an extent that the average in 1940 was less than $600 a year compared with over $1,000 in 1929. The problem which that fact represents is not the farmer's alone; it is a national problem.
I come now to a resolution which deals-with parity of prices. May I read the following resolution passed at the two conventions to which I have already referred1:
Whereas under present conditions primary producers are forced to accept open market prices for their produce and to buy goods which enjoy protected markets;
Whereas this results in the prices of primary products being depressed to minimum levels with the result that the full burden of protection for other industries has to be borne by farmers and other primary producers;
Whereas in addition farmers are obliged to-meet the freight costs of both the goods they sell and the goods they buy;
And whereas this has led to the grave-injustice of the prices of agricultural and other primary products falling in relation to the general price level, thereby divesting such producers of their incomes and causing acute-depression in the primary industries, which in turn threatens the stability of the entire national structure.
Therefore be it resolved that the prices of all primary products, and of farm produce in
Wheat Board Act

particular, be adjusted so as to bear a just relationship to the general price level at all times on the generally accepted basis;
And be it further resolved that in order to meet the injustices created by the present inequitable freight rate structure that freight rates for Canadian goods be equalized on a generally accepted national basis.
I have several other resolutions, minor ones, but I will omit them so that I may have a little more time to devote to other matters. Perhaps the government does not quite get what the farmers mean by parity of prices. There are many explanations of that point. This is what we mean; this is what I mean when I discuss that particular subject. I have in my hand a few clippings from various newspapers from which I will read the headings. Here are several:
Canadian business hits high level; Massey-Harris earns more in 1940; Consolidated Mining earns large profits; Increased profits shown in report of Dominion bank; Hudson's Bay mines profit $5,948,855; C.P.R. earnings up $1,274,000; Canadian Breweries reports $255,931 profit.
That is one side of the story. The other side is this:
Wheat buying unmoved by exports; hog production held losing game.
It is a game to them.
Western farmer faces oversupply period; farmers urged to stress quality.
Some people are not satisfied with the quality though they are getting it for nothing.
Wheat futures touch minimum.
You have the comparison right there, and that is what we mean. The farmer must get a sufficient income to be able to buy the things he needs if he is to get along; to balance consumption with production, we must have parity prices.
The next point I wish to discuss is the debt situation. The hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) dealt with this point and I think he made a good case. The federal government has failed miserably in the protection of our farmers against old private debts. There are literally thousands of farmers throughout western Canada who have been thrust under the heels of financial dictators for the past ten years. These farmers were left at the mercy of soulless financial institutions that were going to get everything out of the iarmers regardless of what may happen to them. This government believes in the sanctity of contracts; oh, yes. In fact, it believes in the sanctity of contracts above the sanctity of homes, and as a result many of our western agriculturists after having toiled for years have been dispossessed of their homes. While travelling throughout the
[Mr. Hlynka.l
country I have examined hundreds of cases which have been reviewed by the boards of review, and I found that in many instances the financial institutions have been charging farmers anywhere from 6 to 14 per cent interest. This government permitted them to bleed the farmers to death, and to-day it is wondering why hon. members representing western agriculture are opposing this particular measure, which will not give the farmer sufficient income to meet his obligations.
At some future date I shall deal with the debt problem at greater length.	On this
occasion I wish to place before the house only one resolution dealing with the debt problem:
Whereas the debts under which the farmers and other people of Canada have been struggling constitute an ever-present threat to their security and a drain on their inadequate resources;
Whereas market conditions, over which they have no control, have forced farmers to produce at prices lower than production costs, thereby leaving them no income with which to meet their obligations;
Whereas provincial debt legislation gave protection to debtors against unjust dispossession of their homes without prejudicing the position of creditors to obtain payment within their debtors' ability to pay;
And whereas the lending institutions have entered upon a course of action which has led to the said acts being declared inoperative by the courts, thereby jeopardizing the property rights of citizens and creating internal disruption at a time when this is most undesirable;
Therefore be it resolved that the federal government be urged to forthwith confer upon provinces any necessary statutory authority which will make the said debt legislation fully operative and beyond the reach of attack by the financial institutions.
And be it further resolved that the federal government be requested to adopt a general revision of debts on the basis of a reduction in the principal amount of outstanding debts by a sum equivalent to any interest payments made prior to December 31, 1936, in excess of 3 per cent simple interest.
That is the third resolution. I have here one further resolution, dealing with interest rates. That has not much to do with the Minister of Agriculture, but while discussing agriculture I believe I should put the resolution on record :
Whereas the farmers are asked to take part in Canada's war effort, and further in view of the fact that farmers' produce is being sold below cost of production;
Therefore be it resolved that this convention go on record demanding that interest on all debts be eliminated for the duration of the war.
These comprise all the resolutions passed at this'convention.
I should like to deal with the debt situation more fully but my time will not permit me to do so now. I just want to say that the

Wheat Board Act
present government has at all times given some excuse for not dealing with debt legislation adequately, for instance, that it would require an amendment to the British North America Act or that it is ultra vires or something of the kind. But this government found no difficulty in bringing in an amendment to the British North America Act when it wanted to put unemployment insurance into effect. The government found no difficulty in invading provincial fields in the matter of income tax and succession duties. But the government finds difficulty when it comes to helping the farmer. The government finds the British North America Act in the way when it comes to old age pensions. Those are the things that I believe the people will eventually have to realize, they will have to learn who their friends are and who are not.
The Minister of Agriculture painted the picture that conditions are going to improve after the war. Let us hope so. But here are three outstanding men who take a different view of agriculture after the war. Here is a clipping from the Calgary Albertan printing a statement by Leonard D. Nesbitt, publicity superintendent of the Alberta wheat pool. He said:
If history repeats itself (and it usually does) a prolonged period of agricultural distress will follow the end of the war. Such a condition has developed after virtually every major war, and particularly during the past century and a half.
One does not need to look back more than two decades to see what happened to agriculture following the first great war. Peace was declared in 1918 and two years of inflation followed. Out of the succeeding nineteen years not less than thirteen have been unfavourable to farmers, in that prices of farm products have been below the prices of other products. In five of these years the difference indicated by comparative indexes amounted to twenty points or more. In all but three of the years, the discrepancy was more than ten points. In only five of the nineteen years did farmers enjoy an advantage, and in none of these did the advantage amount to more than ten points.
Then Professor MacKenzie, president of New Brunswick university, speaking at Montreal on April 11, 1941, is reported as follows:
Speaking of the post-war world, Professor MacKenzie said there would be "disorganization and debts and poverty and suffering ..."
"Taxation will continue," he added, "at high levels, but that in itself need not alarm us, for taxation is merely a method of transferring wealth and of making accumulations of it available for large-scale use."
The last statement is a bit more encouraging, that taxation will be an advantage.
Here is a third quotation, and perhaps the writer, Sir Edward Beatty, is just as important as any of the other gentlemen. In an article
published in the Winnipeg Tribune, of December 31, 1940, he said:
We hear much talk of the social changes that are to follow upon the end of the war. I venture to suggest that the economic changes then experienced will prove more imperative and more immediately effective than any other. It is altogether probable that we shall move into a world that is much poorer than it has been over many generations, and this will apply not only to the fighting nations. For some time to come the countries to which Canada sells products of farm, mine, forest and factory may not he able to pay high prices for their purchases, even though they be in urgent need of the commodities supplied, and it may easily be that our methods of production will have to be raised to new standards of economic efficiency.
These three statements, uttered by men occupying important positions, should perhaps warn the farmers that they had better get matters adjusted for themselves now, otherwise they may find themselves out on the road.
I should now like to say just a word or two about the farmer delegation which visited Ottawa. It is a pity that in time of war there should be even the need for any such delegation. The $35,000 or thereabouts, spent to bring the delegation to Ottawa to plead with the government could have been used to better advantage; but the policies followed by the government during the past ten years-not only by this government but by the one that held office previously, because, after all, there is no difference between the two-placed the farmers in such a position that they were forced to come all this long way in order to make their representation. Personally I would think the best thing would have been for these delegates to see their own members of parliament; to present their demands to them and say, "We want you to bring these matters before the government, and we want results." Believe me, they would have had a number of them climbing up a tree.
In the estimates for 1942-43, tabled a short time ago, I found some startling things. Substantial increases were shown under several headings. Interest on the public debt, and other debt charges, call for instance, for an additional $17,414,000. But there are large decreases in several departments, notably the Department of Agriculture, where the 1942-43 appropriation of $18,508,016 is $30,059,352 less than for 1941-42. Provision for maintenance of prairie farm assistance and rehabilitation measures also was contained in the estimates. Prairie farm rehabilitation and water storage expenses are cut $500,000, but the allocation under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act remains the same at it was last year. The largest reduction was in the amount for wheat acreage reduction payment, $5,225,000 this year as against $35,000,000 last year. Other decreases
Wheat Board Act

are seen in the estimates of the Department *of Pensions and National Health, from $56,799,492 in 1941-42 to $54,839,093 in 1942-43. Then there is a decrease of $573,500 in the cost of old age pensions and pensions for the blind, with $31,372,500 being allocated as the dominion's share of such pensions.
I have the honour to represent the constituency of Vegreville, where we have some of the best young farmers of the west. On several occasions they have won prizes at the International Live Stock Exposition, and following the exposition this year the Associated Press sent out this dispatch:
William Skladan, Andrew, Alberta, kept the oats king title in Canada, with Alex Stewart, Ailsa Craig, Ontario, a former king himself, as runner-up. Dominion exhibitors have w'on the oats award fourteen times in the last twenty-one years.
Paul F. Pawlowski, Vilna, Alberta, who was the oats king last year, lost out in that division but won himself another crown, that of barley king, with Tom Mynzalc, Desjarlais, Alberta, as runner-up.
Then it goes on to say:
Highest award to Canada was that of wheat king, won by William Miller of Edmonton, with R. P. Robbins, Shaunavon, Saskatchewan, as runner-up. Canadians have won this title t-very year since 1928.
The oats king of last year, and the present oats king, both live in the constituency which I represent; yet the strange thing is that though these young farmers win trophies for their wonderful work, they can hardly make a living on the land.
I am sorry that my time is slipping away so quickly, and I shall not have time to deal with other matters of which I should like to speak. In closing, I should like to say that I am glad the government has given consideration to the postponement of military training for farmers' sons. I have had a great number of letters from older folk in my constituency, where perhaps the only son in the family is called up for military service, leaving behind *the parents who are over sixty years of age and unable to work the land. Surely in such cases consideration should, be given, and these young men should be released for spring seeding and other work.
I believe the hon. member for Rosthem dealt very well with the question of the Atlantic charter, so I need not touch upon that matter on this occasion. I should like to add, however-though I do not know whether the word "oomph" is parliamentary- that if the government had put enough *"oomph" into its policies and efforts, I think it could have done a great deal more than it has done. It surely has a great deal of
{Air. Hlynka.]
"oomph" when it comes to political contests. I have never personally met Mr. Arthur Meighen, but he surely must be a terrible man judging by the way he was described in this house. Why, we spent weeks and weeks fighting an election right here in this house, at public expense, getting free publicity. Surely, if there is nothing to be afraid of, the government need not have been so scared.

Mr. Speaker, if the continuation of this debate were to interrupt for one moment the conduct of the war, despite the fact that I do know something about the morale and the condition of affairs on the prairies I assure you I would not occupy the time of the house. I do believe that a people's morale, and their feeling toward their government is important at a time like this.
I was interested this afternoon to hear the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) tell us about his long association with the grain trade, the grain growers and the grain business. Before he had finished1 I was tempted to ask him whether in recent years because of their terrific suffering they had been able to get members of the grain exchange off relief in Winnipeg.
It is unfortunate that the bureau of statistics does not publish facts and figures concerning prices paid to farmers for their grain, and prices finally received by those who sell the grain in the markets of the world. I, too, have been associated with the growing of grain in western Canada since the beginning of the century, and I know something about grain growlers' problems, because I have lived among grain growers. Apparently the minister has lived more in company with those who operate on the grain exchange.
I was sorry to hear the minister point out or even imply this afternoon that there seemed to be some discrimination by one part of Canada against the other parts. In my observations to-day I do not speak only of western agriculture. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) has dealt with parity prices for all agriculture-agriculture	across the whole
dominion. I believe I can speak of agriculture across Canada, because I have been on farms in all but one of the nine provinces, and I know I am stating the truth when I say that agriculture to-day is not receiving parity prices.
Judgment will no doubt be finally passed by those western agriculturists and grain growers in western Canada whose rights the minister was supposed at one time to champion. They will compare the condition of agriculture with the present dismal plight of the grain exchange and of the minister himself.

Wheat Board Act
The amendment before the house states, in effect, that the disregarding by this parliament of the representations made by western agriculture for a parity price for all agricultural products, and of the payment of at least $1 a bushel as an initial price, is contrary to the peace, order and good government of Canada. The resolution deals with the presentation made by western agriculture for a parity price.
I would draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that the parity price is not a cost-plus price; rather it is merely a cost price. The demands for bonuses and other types of assistance would not come at this time if the cost price had existed in the past. The core of the request from western agriculture is the idea of parity, but it should not be taken for granted that the delegation was against bonuses.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) tried to leave the impression in the house that the people were divided, that one group was asking for a bonus on a bushelage basis while the other was asking for one on an acreage basis. That is an unfair suggestion, because I do not believe that at any time the delegation made any such submission.

speechtext:
In the memorandum submitted it will be found that they were asking for a continuation and expansion of the principle of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I believe the government has done that. There are new bonuses by order in council -though heaven knows how long they will last. Payments made under the w'heat acreage reduction bonus are a form of income insurance. The request for a parity price is a request for a fair wage, and that is about all. I suppose we could call the bonus a form of unemployment insurance, the only difference being that whether or not the farmer gets a crop he must still do the work. The income insurance is protection against receiving nothing for the work he does.
The delegation was one of which I say Canadians might well be proud. It was one consisting not only of agriculturists, but including people from almost all walks of life, people representing almost every phase of economic life in the western provinces. There were mayors of cities, reeves of municipalities, clergymen, teachers, storekeepers, businessmen, and the legislature of Saskatchewan was represented. Anyone hearing them was at once convinced that they were speaking with the calm assurance of people asking for justice. Their cause was a just and righteous one, and one which gave them strength. In my opinion the only reason why we did not have a similar delegation from all the provinces, was that agriculture is not organized across the dominion. If it were organized effectively across Canada there would have been deputations from all the provinces. I would like every hon. member to realize that those people would not have come to the capital city at this time, a time when our nation, our empire and democracy is in danger, unless they were filled with the righteousness of their cause, and knew that conditions were desperate. That is positive proof that there is something deeply wrong with agricultural economy in Canada.
From the evidence submitted by the delegation it is clear that a continuance of conditions in western agriculture will undermine the whole economy. I am sorry the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has not seen fit to make a statement to the house respecting this matter, because he was very much in evidence during the time the delegation was here. Ministers of the crown who met with and spoke to the delegation admitted that the case presented was fair and reasonable.
Unless agriculture can obtain the cost of production, it must be condemned to tenant peasantry. If one cannot get the cost of production from his work, then the industry with which he is connected is headed for bankruptcy. Agriculture has been headed for bankruptcy for so many years that the fault is deep-rooted. Anyone who knows about the debt situation of agriculture in western Canada will know that it carries a debt load of about $S00,000.000. The destruction of our ownership of our homes will be the natural consequence of a continuation of this policy. The home is the foundation of any country. No people ever rose in the scale of nations if they let their agricultural economy sink to a level where the people could no longer live decently in homes of their own. Sixty years ago from seventy to eighty per cent of the people of Canada used to live under the healthy conditions of their farm homes, but now probably not more than forty per cent live on the land. This is a sign of inward decay of the nation. Migration of people from the farms to the city is a dangerous sign of decay. It should not be permitted in any nation; it should not be permitted by those who claim to be the governors of that nation.
It is not that people do not want to live on the farms, because they enjoy living there. If you will give some form of security, the people will live there. Something drastic will have to be done sooner or later to change our economy and make it possible for these people to live decently. The decision of the cabinet and the wheat committee, whoever they are, not to grant a parity price is merely a sacrificing of these people. We are destroying their last vestige of hope. Apparently the grain exchange is to continue. Apparently
Wheat Board Act

the packing plants and the packing houses are to continue to fatten upon the live stock brought in by the producers.
The farmer finds that he is losing whatever equity he had in his farm. He is finally forced to give up the lifelong struggle to keep his head above water. Every two or three days I receive communications from people in the west telling me of foreclosure actions against their farms. In some cases the sons who had kept things going as the parents got older have enlisted. I ask hon. members to consider how these boys in the forces must feel when they receive word from their parents at home that they no longer own the land. They are fortunate if they are allowed to stay on as tenants of the mortgage companies. It is much worse when the older people are turned out and have to depend upon charity.
I cannot understand why we should have to plead on the floor of this house for a parity price. It is only common justice that this should be given; it is the very essence of justice and fairness. It should fall like the rain and the sunshine upon everyone; it should be a recognized right. A continued lack of parity prices has left the farmer in a position of debt. I think I am quite safe in saying that for the last twelve years agriculture has not received its cost of production. As has been said by almost every speaker, the debt situation in the country is intolerable. There is something fundamentally wrong with a system which permits debt to rise.
A farmer requires a certain amount of capital to carry on his work of production, and he must give also the labour of himself and his family. Both of these should be rewarded if there is any production. The farmer uses the labour of his family and himself to produce, and the capital is used to buy the machinery which is needed for production. But if, because of circumstances beyond his control, the farmer loses his crop by frost, drought, hail, grasshoppers, rust or some other calamity, he receives no returr for his labour that year. The farmer gets absolutely nothing for his labour, but with the institutions as they are organized in this country, capital receives a reward that year. If the farmer cannot pay his interest, then it is piled on to the debt, and the next year he is penalized for not having produced the year before when it was not his fault that he could not. That same year the machinery produced no -wheat, but the next year or the year after, the farmer must pay double toll. The reward of capital is too great while the reward of labour is negligible. This accumulation of debt is crushing this industry.
[Mr. Castleden.l
The debt legislation that we have in the provinces does not meet the problem at all. Even though parity prices were granted, I do not believe the farmers of western Canada in the next ten years could work their way out from under the burden of debt that is placed upon them. But when the administration says that they will not recognize the claims to parity, then there can be no hope because the cost of production is not there. The burden of debt will continue and it will pyramid. This problem will have to be met. I think in war time the government should at least recognize that the solving of this problem is an essential step in the peace, order and good government of this country.

There is also the matter of storage of grain in privately leased elevators. The Dominion of Canada built these terminals at a tremendous cost to the country, and then, instead of operating them and controlling them, leased them to grain companies, members of the grain exchange, at rentals as low as $72,000 or $73,000 a year, that figure being accepted for the use of an elevator holding three to three and a quarter million bushels of grain. We permit the grain companies, some of them with offices outside the dominion, to make hundreds of thousands of dollars by storing Canadian wheat in elevators belonging to the Canadian people. I should think that with the development which has gone on in twenty or thirty years there would be practically no more space to fill up in the three western provinces. If my information is correct, only about eighteen million acres of land in those western provinces are fit for cultivation, and a lot of that is sub-marginal. Therefore on that score alone one can easily see the turmoil and the travail of the western deputations who are discussing the problem of agriculture, and the time may not be far distant when the west will have to go into subsistence farming.
At this point I should like to say a few words about the delegation which was in Ottawa a few weeks ago. My personal belief is that it was one of the finest movements of farmers this country has ever seen. Everyone will admire them, and particularly when we remember that these large and small rural municipalities which suffered1 so much during the depression, which have suffered from {Mr. Bradette.]
drought during many years, and from debts, found it possible to raise a sum of money large enough to send to Ottawa a delegation so representative and in such large numbers. I believe, however, that if they had seen their own good, clean-cut and active members of parliament discussing their problems, with the vim and fervour that they always display, they would have realized that the question of agriculture was being well handled and brought before national attention on the floor of the house.
When I say that the western members are vocal I do not make the statement disparagingly. It is their duty as impartially but as strongly as possible to bring before the house the great problems they face. But I make this one appeal; I want you to give us a chance to appreciate and understand the problems of others also. I must say, however, that I will vote against the amendment of the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) for the very good reason that I cannot see the necessity for it. He might just as easily have asked for $1.10 or $1.20 as have asked for $1. That 10 cents would mean an awful lot to the farmers in the three western provinces, or to farmers in Ontario. At the same time, however, the hon. member for Weyburn is a logical and practical individual, because he has been dealing with spiritual matters, and also with matters of the body, and he knows that all our wishes cannot come through.
I say we cannot always get what we want in this world. I know I have always applied that principle to myself. We have to be reasonable and fair. The western agriculturist is as great a realist as you will find; he is just as practical as any other man in Canada. The delegation was well received-in fact I believe it was received by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and1 by several cabinet ministers and members of parliament. I had the pleasure of meeting quite a number of those who came, and I was agreeably astonished to see the number of French-Canadians in the group. Among the French-Canadians -I believe there were twenty or twenty-four of them-there were three or four Belgians. How proud I was to see their intense Cana-dianism and their great pride in affiliation with us!
When we are dealing with this subject we ought not to bring any politics into it. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) said the other day that he believed there was politics in this kind of legislation and the reception of that delegation. If I wished to enlarge upon that angle, I would remind the hon. member of the discussion which took place in 1931 with respect to the
